System

Everything our installed phone apps and Mac apps are built from: seven rules, one set of tokens, and the elements, each through six gates.

00

Ground rules

Seven rules. Each one is checkable, and tools/check.mjs checks the ones a machine can.

  1. Two line weights.

    2px frames what you press or what contains. 1px only divides. A heavier 4px exists for forced-colours and nothing else.

  2. Flat.

    No gradients, no blur, no glass, and one translucency only: the scrim behind a modal. A shadow is hard-edged and means “you can press this”. Hover and press never move the hit box.

  3. Rectangles hold, circles act.

    Containers are square rectangles. Buttons and handles are circles or pills. Two exceptions: the card bar's small square control, and the checkbox, which every platform draws square.

  4. Uppercase is structure.

    Bar labels and index numbers. Everything you read is sentence case.

  5. Say something real.

    No lorem ipsum, no “John Doe”, no “seamless”. Copy comes from the product.

  6. Colour is a swap.

    Components read roles: --paper, --ink, --tone-3. Only tokens/color*.css knows a colour value.

  7. No decoration.

    If it carries no information and offers no action, it goes. No dotted backgrounds, no icons in tinted circles.

Put data-tone="1" to "6" or "ink" on a card: six greys, 1 the quietest, in the same order in both schemes. The accent is ink until an app sets its own, checked by tools/accent.mjs.

02

Elements

Everything a phone app or a Mac app needs, in the order it's being built. Each element gets a page here and a spec in elements/. Colour, motion and the freeze then pass over all of them together.

Element What it's for Status
Card One idea in a frame: a deck, a stat, a row, the flashcard itself. Gates 0–3
Button Every action: primary, secondary, quiet, destructive, icon-only. Gates 0–3
Field Typing: text, search, number, several lines, with a label, help and an error. Gates 0–3
Tag and Badge A status word on a thing, and a count on a control. Gates 0–3
Meter and Spinner How far along, and “working on it” when nobody knows how long. Gates 0–3
Icons The glyph set: line work on the frame’s 2px weight. Gates 0–3
Checkbox Independent on/off choices. Gates 0–3
Radio One choice from a short list. Gates 0–3
Switch A setting that takes effect at once. Gates 0–3
Segmented control One of two to four views or modes, side by side. Gates 0–3
Select One choice from a long list, in the platform’s own picker. Gates 0–3
Stepper A small number, one step at a time. Gates 0–3
Form Fields together: groups, help, errors and the submit row. Gates 0–3
Frame The app shell: safe areas, bars and the scroll region. Gates 0–3
Top bar A screen’s title, its back control and one or two actions. Gates 0–3
Tab bar The three to five places at the root of a phone app. Gates 0–3
Sidebar Navigation on wide screens, and the split view. Gates 0–3
List Rows of things, with swipe actions that also have a visible button. Gates 0–3
Tabs Sections of one screen. Gates 0–3
Disclosure Show more, in place. Gates 0–3
Menu A short list of actions behind one control. Gates 0–3
Dialog Stop and decide: confirm or acknowledge. Gates 0–3
Sheet A task on top of a screen; from the bottom on a phone. Gates 0–3
Toast It’s done, with Undo. Gates 0–3
Banner News about the whole screen: offline, an update ready, a failure. Gates 0–3
Empty, loading and error What a screen shows before there’s anything, and when something fails. Gates 0–3
PWA platform Install, offline, updates, permissions, sharing and the keyboard. Gates 0–3

After the elements: colour and dark mode (wave 6, gate 3), motion (wave 7, gate 4), then the freeze (wave 8, gate 5).

Cards

A card holds one idea. The frame is fixed; what goes inside is a slot. This chapter is structure only: greys, hard lines, no motion.

Show boxes
01

Anatomy

Nine parts, all optional except the frame. A card is whichever of them it needs.

1

07 — Diamond

Image 4:3

Shape 07

Diamond

Taller than it is wide, on purpose. Equal diagonals is just a square on its corner.

Seen on Tuesday
  1. 1
    Frame.card

    2px, --card-line. Clips its contents, and is the container that cqi and @container card measure against.

  2. 2
    Bar.card__bar

    The frame made thicker: ink fill, a label on the left, one control on the right. The control is a 44px target around a 20px box.

  3. 3
    Media.card__media

    Edge to edge, 4:3 unless --ratio says otherwise. Closed off by a 2px rule, never a shadow.

  4. 4
    Body.card__body

    Where the padding lives: clamp(1rem, 5cqi, 1.5rem), so a narrow card is snug and a wide one breathes.

  5. 5
    Eyebrow.card__eyebrow

    14px, soft ink. Says what kind of thing this is.

  6. 6
    Title.card__title

    Weight 500, 22 to 32px depending on the card's width. Balanced, so it never leaves one word on its own line.

  7. 7
    Text.card__text

    16px on a 1.5 line, 40 characters wide at most.

  8. 8
    Foot.card__foot

    A 1px rule, then the small print. Sticks to the bottom, so cards in a row end on one line. A link in it gets the full 44px target.

  9. 9
    Action.card__action

    A 44px circle. Round means it does something, so it is always a real button. In a ghost card it marks the card, which is the button.

02

Variants

Eight cards, one idea each. The markup under every specimen is read from the live element, so it can't drift from what you're looking at.

  • Box with an X: an image goes here
  • Flat grey: a tone slot
  • Ink: the inverted tone
  • Dashed: empty, or not yet
  • Hatch: disabled

2.6

Link

The whole card goes somewhere.

.card--link .card__link

One anchor, in the title, stretched over the card with ::after. One tab stop, one accessible name, and the whole card is the target. The card wears the focus ring, not the anchor. Ghost

The empty slot that asks to be filled.

.card--ghost

Dashed means nothing here yet. The card is the anchor or the button itself. On hover and on focus alike it firms up and lifts.

2.8

Study

The flashcard itself. 5:7, one subject, one hint.

.card--study .card__stage .card__answer

Static faces only. The flip is motion, so it's designed at gate 4: perspective on the parent, backfaces hidden, cubic-bezier(.83, 0, .17, 1), and under reduced motion a short crossfade instead. The card never grows taller than the screen: inside a Frame, --chrome is measured for you; outside one, set it to the height of the bars. It never gets narrower than 8rem.

The .is-* classes force a state for this page and for tests. They are not API: real states come from :hover (only where a pointer hovers), :focus-visible, :active, aria-current on a card's link, aria-selected on a card that is an option in a listbox, and the .card--disabled modifier.

4.3

Container sizing

A card answers to its own width, not the window.

cqi @container card

Element 02ColourGates 0 to 3 done

Buttons

A button starts an action. It is a pill because it acts, it is always 44px tall, and its words say what will happen.

01

Variants

One size, one shape, three levels of emphasis. Every variant is a real <button> with .btn; the modifiers only change what it looks like at rest.

1.1

Primary

The one thing to press in this part of the screen.

.btn .btn--primary

Filled with --accent and --on-accent (ink and paper until an app sets its own). At most one per region: if two things both want to be primary, one of them isn't.

Two regions, one primary each.

1.2

Secondary

Everything else that deserves a frame.

.btn

The default: .btn with no modifier is a 2px ink frame on paper. A leading icon is optional and comes before the label.

1.3

Quiet

For bars and card feet, where a frame would be noise.

.btn .btn--quiet

No frame until hover or focus, but the full 44px target and the same padding, so the label sits where a framed one would. Next to a primary it is the way out.

Deck · 12 cards

Shapes

1.4

Destructive

Something that can't be taken back.

.btn .btn--quiet

A recipe, not a class. The words carry it: a verb and the thing it destroys. Never primary, never red (the palette is monochrome, for good). It always asks first, as here, or offers Undo afterwards.

First press. Opens the question.

Delete Shapes?

Its 12 cards and what you've learned go with it.

The question. The way out is quiet, the loss is named.

1.5

Icon-only

When the glyph says it all, and space is short.

.btn--icon aria-label

A 44px circle. The button carries the aria-label; the icon is aria-hidden. Works with any emphasis: framed by default, quiet in a bar.

1.6

Toggle

An action that stays on until you turn it off.

aria-pressed

The label never changes; aria-pressed says on or off. On doubles the frame, as a selected card does, and shows a check, so it can't be mistaken for focus or for a primary. Press one to try it.

1.7

Block

The full width of a phone form.

.btn--block

Takes the width of its column, nothing more. On a wide screen the column is narrow, so the button is too.

1.8

Busy

The press was heard, and the work takes a moment.

aria-busy .spinner

The label stays; there is no "Loading…" text. A spinner (from Meter) takes the leading icon's place, it stops lifting, and the app ignores another press until the work is done.

Before.

Busy. Same label, same width.

1.9

A row of buttons

Two or three choices side by side.

.btn-row

12px apart, so targets never touch. The primary goes last, at the trailing end, as on the Mac and iOS. Block buttons in a row share it equally and stack when each would be under three targets wide.

The study screen. Shared, equal widths.

A deck. Each as wide as its words.

02

States

The card's two numbers: --lift draws the hard shadow, --fill swaps ink and paper. Rest is flat, hover lifts, press goes back down and keeps the fill. Secondary, primary and quiet in each.

Rest. Flat. The pill already says it can be pressed.

Hover. Filled, with a 4px hard shadow. Nothing moves.

Focus. The hover look, plus a 3px ring 3px out.

Pressed. Back down: the shadow goes, the fill stays, and a 2px ring shows inside the frame, so even a primary answers a tap.

Selected. A toggle that's on: the frame doubles and a check shows. Here at rest and hovered.

Add a card to this deck first.

Disabled. Dashed and faint, still focusable, and it says why. Prefer not disabling at all.

The .is-* classes force a state for this page and for tests. They are not API: real states come from :hover (only where a pointer hovers), :focus-visible, :active, aria-pressed, aria-busy and aria-disabled.

03

Usage

A button reads the surface it sits on. In a card it takes the card's ink and fill, so the same markup works on paper, on a tone and on the inverted tone.

3.1

On a card

The same buttons on paper, a tone and ink.

--card-ink --card-bg

On the ink card the frame, the label and the shadow all turn paper. The card's own round action and square bar control stay the card's for now: the spec says how they line up.

Colours

Carry on

Shapes

On the tone and ink cards the second button is held in its hover look, to show the lift on each surface.

  1. Do

    Start the label with a verb and name the thing: "Add a shape", "Delete deck". Keep it to two or three words. One primary per region, last in the row.

  2. Don't

    Don't disable a button to say "not yet": leave it on and explain when it's pressed. Don't make a link look like a button unless it goes somewhere you'd start from. Don't put a shadow on it at rest.

  3. Destructive

    The words carry it, never a colour. Ask first, or do it and offer Undo. A destructive button is never the primary.

  4. Installed PWA

    Touch has no hover, so the pressed look (fill and inner ring) is the feedback; the shell's touchstart listener turns on :active in iOS Safari. touch-action: manipulation removes the double-tap wait.

  5. Mac and SwiftUI

    System chrome (toolbar, alerts, sheets) keeps system buttons; ours are for content. In SwiftUI, one custom ButtonStyle reads configuration.isPressed, hover and focus, and draws the same capsule.

Element 03ColourGates 0 to 3 done

Field

Lets someone type one value. A square frame, because it holds text; a label that never goes away; and an error that says how to fix it, without needing colour.

01

Anatomy

Six parts. Only the label and the input are always there. Help and error sit between them, above the input, where the on-screen keyboard can't cover them.

Shown on the deck's card.

Give the deck a name

5 6
  1. 1
    Label.field__label

    A real <label for>, above the input, always visible. 16px, weight 600, sentence case. Never replaced by the placeholder.

  2. 2
    Help.field__help

    14px, soft ink. Tied to the input with aria-describedby.

  3. 3
    Error.field__error

    A warning glyph and the fix, in words: 16px, weight 600. Listed first in aria-describedby; the input gets aria-invalid="true".

  4. 4
    Input.field__input

    A 2px square frame, 44px tall, 16px text. Wrapped in .field__box only when an icon or a clear button sits in it. Invalid doubles the frame.

  5. 5
    Leading icon.field__icon

    Decorative and aria-hidden. Clicks go through it to the input.

  6. 6
    Clear button.field__clear

    A real <button> with aria-label="Clear search": a 44px target around a 28px circle. Round, because it acts.

02

Variants

Four, and they share everything but the input: the same frame, label, help and error. Each one asks the phone for the right keyboard and the right Return key.

2.1

Text

One short line: a name, a title.

.field .field__label .field__help .field__input

type="text", autocomplete="off" (a deck name isn't personal data, so no browser suggestions), enterkeyhint="done", or "next" when another field follows.

Shown on the deck's card. You can change it later.

2.2

Search

Narrows a list as you type.

.field__box .field__icon .field__clear

type="search" inside <search>, enterkeyhint="search", autocomplete="off", autocapitalize="none". The clear button shows only while there's text: the app toggles hidden, empties the field and puts focus back in it. Escape clears too, natively. The placeholder is an example, not the label.

2.3

Number

A count you'd rather type than step to.

.field--number

type="text" with inputmode="numeric" and pattern="[0-9]*": the number pad, no spinner arrows, and no scroll wheel changing the value by accident. Its width hints at the answer. The range goes in the help, and the check happens on submit.

From 5 to 50.

2.4

Multi-line

A few sentences.

textarea.field__input

A <textarea>, four rows to start. It resizes downwards only and keeps its scroll to itself. enterkeyhint="enter", because Return makes a new line here.

Only you see these.

03

States

Seven states, all from the input itself. A field isn't pressed, so it never lifts: hover changes its ground, focus rings it. Grey only, so every state has to read without colour.

Shown on the deck's card.

Rest. A 2px frame on paper.

Shown on the deck's card.

Hover. The ground turns to canvas. Pointers only, and never on a field you can't type in.

Shown on the deck's card.

Focus. A 3px ring, 3px out. Mouse or keyboard alike: the caret is there either way.

Shown on the deck's card.

Filled. Ink text. Nothing else changes: the label stays where it was.

Shown on the deck's card.

Give the deck a name

Invalid. The frame doubles, and a glyph and the fix sit above it. No red: there isn't any.

Finish the current session to change this.

Disabled. Dashed and faint, out of the tab order, and the help says why.

Built-in decks keep their name. Duplicate it to rename it.

Read-only. No box: a value on a 1px rule. You can still focus it, select it and copy it.

The clear button

Rest. A 2px circle: round, because it acts.

Hover. It fills with ink.

Focus. The ring hugs the circle and stays inside the frame.

Pressed. Filled, as on hover, so a tap answers too.

The .is-* classes force a state for this page and for tests. They are not API: real states come from :hover (only where a pointer hovers), :focus-visible, :active, aria-invalid, disabled and readonly.

04

Usage

  1. Do

    Name the thing in the label ("Deck name", not "Name"). Put the range or the rule in the help. Write the error as the fix: "Give the deck a name", not "Required".

  2. Don't

    Don't use the placeholder as the label: it vanishes on the first letter. Don't disable a field without saying why next to it; read-only, or leaving it out, is usually kinder.

  3. Installed PWA

    16px text or more, or iOS zooms on focus. inputmode and enterkeyhint pick the keyboard and its Return key. Help and error sit above the input, so the keyboard never hides them.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    The toolbar's search is the system's own field (.searchable); ours are for content. In SwiftUI, a TextField with a custom style: a 2pt square stroke, our label above, the system focus ring.

Tags

A tag is a status word on a thing. A badge is a count on a control. Neither can be pressed, so neither is round.

01

Variants

Tags take the system's tones: none, ink, or 1 to 6. The badge has one look: an ink square with a number in it.

1.1

Tag

Where a card stands: known, new, due, not yet.

.tag

A square 2px frame around one or two words in label type. The markup stays sentence case ("Not yet"); the capitals are CSS, so a screen reader says the words, not the letters. It replaced the wireframe kit's stand-in.

Known New Due Not yet

1.2

Ink

The one status on the screen that has to be seen first.

data-tone="ink"

The surface's ink and fill swap, so on an ink card it turns paper instead of vanishing. Use it sparingly: if every tag is ink, none is.

Due Known Known

1.3

Tones

Six grey fills, 1 the quietest, in either scheme.

data-tone="1" … "6"

Rhythm, not meaning. The word says "Due"; a tone never says it alone. Text and frame take the slot's own ink, --on-tone-N.

New New Due Due Known Not yet

Where tags live most: the end of a row.

1.5

Badge

How many are waiting behind a control.

.badge aria-hidden

At least 20px, ink, tabular figures, and "99+" past 99. Pinned to the corner of an icon button; after the label in a text button. The badge is aria-hidden: the count is in the control's name, so it is heard as "Decks, 7 due".

02

States

None of their own: no hover, focus or press, because neither acts. A tag changes with the surface under it; a badge changes with its count, and follows its control's state.

KnownDueNew

On paper. The frame and words are ink.

KnownDueNew

On a tone. No fill of its own: the tone shows through.

KnownDueNew

On ink. Frame and words turn paper; the ink tag turns paper.

One, two and three figures. It widens; past 99 it stops.

On a hovered or pressed control. The 2px cut keeps it apart from the fill.

Zero. No badge at all, and no count in the name.

03

Usage

  1. Do

    Use the product's own status words, one or two: Known, New, Due, Not yet. Put the true count in the control's name and cap only what's drawn.

  2. Don't

    Don't make a tag pressable. A filter is a toggle button or a segmented control. Don't let a tone carry a status on its own, and don't badge something that has no count.

  3. Installed PWA

    The home-screen badge is the system's, set through the Badging API (wave 5). It and the in-app badge show the same number.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    A tag is Text in the label style with a square strokeBorder. A system tab or sidebar row takes the system .badge(_:); our own controls draw this one, with the count in .accessibilityLabel.

Element 05ColourGates 0 to 3 done

Meters

How far along, and “working on it” when nobody knows how long. A bar never stands alone: it always comes with a name and the amount in words.

01

Variants

Three bars, one look: a square 2px frame filled from the start edge, the name on the left, the amount on the right. Which one is a question of meaning, not looks.

1.1

Meter

A value in a range: how much of a deck you know.

.meter .meter__bar role="meter"

The bar is labelled by the name and speaks its aria-valuetext, the same words you see. So the visible amount is aria-hidden and is heard once. --value sets the fill. It replaced the wireframe kit's stand-in.

Progress

03

Usage

  1. Do

    Name what's measured and say the amount the way a person would: "5 of 12 known", not "42%". If you can count it, show progress, not a spinner.

  2. Don't

    Don't show a bar without its words, a spinner without its words, or a meter where a number alone would do. Don't use segments past 20 cards.

  3. Installed PWA

    Offline, nothing loads from the network: say what's on the device instead of spinning. A long import keeps its progress on screen, so a person can leave and come back.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    ProgressView(value:total:) with a custom style for progress, Gauge for a meter. In system chrome the system spinner stays; in content, this ring, always with a Text.

Icons

Twenty-six glyphs, drawn as line work on the frame's own weight: a 24 grid, a 2px stroke with square ends, no fills. They take the colour of the text around them.

01

The set

Each glyph at 48, 24 and 20px. The 48 is there to show the drawing; 20px (--ic-size: 1.25rem, the default) and 24px are the sizes in use. Every one is a --icon-* token and an .ic--* class; the path data, for native apps, is in icons.md.

1.1

Navigation

Moving around inside the app.

.ic--back .ic--forward .ic--down .ic--up

Chevrons, not arrows: they move you within the app, and ↗ is kept for leaving it. Back sits in the top bar with the previous screen's name; forward ends a row that opens a screen.

1.2

Actions

Something you do to the thing on screen.

.ic--more .ic--search .ic--edit .ic--delete .ic--share .ic--undo .ic--refresh .ic--shuffle .ic--flip .ic--install .ic--sidebar

Each one is the glyph for one verb, so it never changes meaning between screens. Delete always has words beside it ("Delete deck"). Share is also where iOS keeps Add to Home Screen.

1.3

Status

News about the app or a field.

.ic--info .ic--warning .ic--offline

Always next to words: "You're offline. Changes are saved on this device." The glyph is a second cue, never the only one. Drawn a little larger than the square glyphs, because a circle and a triangle look smaller at the same width.

1.4

Places

The tab bar and the sidebar.

.ic--settings .ic--today .ic--decks

Settings is a pair of sliders, not a gear: at 20px a gear's teeth close up into a blob, and sliders stay two clean lines. Decks is a stack of cards. In a tab bar the label always sits beside the glyph.

1.5

Kept from v0

The first five, unchanged.

.ic--arrow .ic--plus .ic--minus .ic--close .ic--check

Same class names, same drawings. ↗ (arrow) means "leaves the app", on the web and on Apple platforms, so it never marks an in-app link.

02

In use

A glyph has no states of its own: it takes currentColor from the control or the text it sits in, so it follows them through hover, press, the inverted tone and forced colours.

2.1

Two sizes

20px beside text, 24px on its own.

--ic-size

20px (1.25rem) is the default: in fields, lists and beside a label. 24px (1.5rem) where the glyph stands alone in a bar. Both are rem, so they grow with the reader's text size. Smaller only inside a drawn box, as in the card's bar control.

20px. --ic-size: 1.25rem, the default.

24px. --ic-size: 1.5rem, standing alone.

2.2

Inline with text

A glyph inside a sentence.

--ic-size: 1.25em

Sized in em so it follows the line, and lowered by vertical-align: -0.25em so it centres on the capitals. Inside a flex row (a control, a field) none of this is needed: align-items: center does it.

To install it, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen.

You're offline. Changes are saved on this device.

Archivo is under the SIL Open Font License

↗ only on a link that leaves the app. In-app links get no glyph.

2.3

In a control

A glyph is the whole visible label.

aria-label aria-hidden

The control carries the name ("Share Shapes"); the glyph stays aria-hidden. The target is 44px whatever the glyph's size. Shown in Button's icon-only control, and in the card's own slots: the 20px box of the bar control and the 44px action circle.

Deck

12 cards

Shapes

5 of 12 known

2.4

Ink and forced colours

Any ground, any theme.

currentColor CanvasText

On the inverted tone a glyph is paper because its text is. In forced colours (Windows contrast themes) backgrounds are dropped, and a mask glyph is a background, so icons.css paints every glyph in CanvasText there, in every state. No glyph needs colour to read, so nothing else changes.

03

Usage

  1. Do

    Mark every glyph aria-hidden="true": it is decoration. When a glyph is a control's only content, name the control with aria-label. Pair status glyphs with words.

  2. Don't

    Don't put a glyph in a tinted circle, or repeat one on every card in a grid. Don't use ↗ for an in-app link. Don't fill or tint a glyph to make it mean something.

  3. Installed PWA

    No browser chrome, so back is always on screen. iOS keeps Add to Home Screen behind its Share sheet: install instructions show the share glyph. Chromium's prompt gets the install glyph.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    Native toolbars and menus use SF Symbols; these are for what we draw. In SwiftUI each glyph is a Path on the 24 grid, stroked with lineWidth: 2 and lineCap: .square.

Variants

Four, all the same box. A checkbox is a choice you make now and that counts when the form is sent; a setting that acts the moment you touch it is a switch.

2.1

Single

One choice, yes or no.

The words say what checked means: "Show hints", not "Hints". The input sits inside its label, so the label needs no for.

2.2

Group

Several choices that answer one question.

.checkbox-group .field__label .field__help

A <fieldset> with a <legend>, one name for all the boxes. Each box is its own tab stop; Space toggles it. Options are 8px apart, so two 44px targets never touch.

Decks to study

Mixed

"All decks", over a group where only some are checked.

:indeterminate aria-controls

Mixed exists only in script: input.indeterminate = true, and screen readers hear "mixed". The box lists the boxes it controls in aria-controls. Checking it checks them all; a press in the mixed state checks all, as natively. Try it: this one is live.

Two numbers draw them, as on the card: --lift is a 2px hard shadow, --fill is the box's ground. Checked and mixed carry a glyph too, so each state reads in grey and in forced colours.

04

Usage

  1. Do

    Say what checked means, in the positive: "Show hints", not "Hide hints" or "Hints". Put a group's question in its legend, and use a checkbox when the choice counts on Save.

  2. Don't

    Don't use a checkbox for something that happens at once: that's a switch. Don't use one for a single choice from a list: that's a radio. Don't round it, and don't put the help inside the label.

  3. Installed PWA

    The whole label is the target, so a thumb on the words toggles it. Pressed fills the box at once, so a tap answers on a screen with no hover.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    Space toggles; Tab moves box to box. In SwiftUI, a Toggle with a custom ToggleStyle that draws the square; on the Mac, .toggleStyle(.checkbox) in system chrome.

04

Usage

  1. Do

    Ask the question in the legend ("Card order") and keep each option to a few words. Order options in a way that means something: the usual first, or least to most.

  2. Don't

    Don't use radios for one yes-or-no: that's a checkbox. Don't go past six options: that's a select. Don't make a radio do something the moment it's chosen.

  3. Installed PWA

    The words are part of the target, so a thumb anywhere on the row chooses. Pressed inks the circle at once, so a tap answers on a screen with no hover.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    Tab reaches the group once; arrows choose. In SwiftUI, a Picker with .pickerStyle(.radioGroup) on the Mac; on iOS a custom row with our circle, since iOS has no native radio.

04

Usage

  1. Do

    Name the setting, not the action: "Daily reminder", not "Turn on reminders". Make it take effect the moment it flips, and show the effect where it can be seen.

  2. Don't

    Don't put a switch in a form with Save or Cancel: use a checkbox. Don't write On or Off inside the track, and don't let the words beside it be the only change.

  3. Installed PWA

    The whole row is the target, as in iOS Settings. A setting that needs a permission (notifications) asks first, in our words, before the system prompt.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    Space flips it. In SwiftUI, a Toggle with a custom ToggleStyle that draws the pill and the word; on the Mac, system settings in system chrome keep .toggleStyle(.switch).

The .is-* classes force a state for this page and for tests. They are not API: real states come from :hover (only where a pointer hovers), :focus-visible, :active, aria-disabled (set by the script at a limit), aria-invalid and disabled.

04

Usage

  1. Do

    Use it for a small range in even steps, where nudging beats typing. Put the range in the help, and name the buttons for what they do: "Fewer cards", "More cards".

  2. Don't

    Don't hide or truly disable a button at a limit: it stays, says why, and keeps focus. Don't use it for a wide range or exact values; that's a number field.

  3. Installed PWA

    The value brings up the number pad. Button's touch-action: manipulation lets quick taps on More cards step instead of zooming the page.

  4. Mac and SwiftUI

    Up and Down step from the value, as in a Mac number field. In SwiftUI, our circles and a TextField on iOS; the system's Stepper beside the field on the Mac.

    How spaced repetition works

    Each card comes back just before you'd forget it. Get one right and it waits longer next time: a day, then three, then a week. Get it wrong and it comes back tomorrow.

    So a session is short. Today's seven cards in Shapes take about three minutes, and the ones you already know stay out of the way until they're due again.

    A streak counts the days you finished what was due. Miss a day and nothing is lost: the cards wait, and tomorrow's session is a little longer.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

      One frame per screen, as the first thing in <body> after the skip link, with the scroll region as the <main>. Keep the order top bar, content, bottom bar, so Tab goes the way the eye does. Load dist/flashcards.js for --chrome.

    2. Don't

      Don't let the page scroll behind the frame, read --safe-* in content, or float a bar over the content: bars run edge to edge and clip what scrolls. Don't use position: fixed inside the frame for overlays; a dialog, sheet or menu goes in the top layer (<dialog>, popover).

    3. Installed PWA

      Needs viewport-fit=cover, or every safe area is 0, and interactive-widget=resizes-content, so Android ends the frame at the keyboard. The frame is the one thing sized in dvh; the page never scrolls, so the browser's bars stay put in a tab too. While the keyboard is up the Tab bar hides (frame.js sets data-keyboard), so the field has the room.

    4. Mac and SwiftUI

      In a Mac window the toolbar and sidebar are the system's, so the content is a frame with no bars (see Screens). In SwiftUI the frame is the scene: NavigationStack or NavigationSplitView with .safeAreaInset(edge:) for an action row.

    Usage

      Not on a Mac: places there are the system sidebar. In SwiftUI it's a TabView with a .tabItem (a Label) per place and .badge(_:) for the count; the system draws it.

    02

    Variants

    Two frames (plain and inset) and four kinds of row. The boxes here are a phone's width; the outline stands for the screen's edges.

    2.1

    Plain

    Rows straight on the screen: a deck's numbers, search results.

    .list .list__rows .list__row .list__main .list__title .list__trail

    Edge to edge: straight in a Frame's scroll region it reaches over the region's side padding, and its rows take that padding, so their text lines up with the content above. Elsewhere its rows keep the screen's --gutter, and rules close it top and bottom, so its edges show without colour. A row that only shows a value is a <div> and has no states.

    2.2

    Inset

    A group that belongs together: a deck's settings, one screen's few links.

    .list--inset

    Panel-style: a square 2px frame on paper, inside the screen's gutter, with 16px in the rows. A frame contains, so it's 2px; the rules inside only divide, so they're 1px.

    2.3

    With section headers

    A long screen in a few named parts: decks by what's due, settings by topic.

    .list__head

    One .list per section, each with its heading inside; sections stack 24px apart. Plain, the heading is a label over the rule. Inset, it is the Panel's bar. Use real heading elements, in order, so the screen can be skimmed by heading.

    2.4

    Row as a link

    Each row opens something: a deck, a card, a setting's own screen.

    a.list__row .list__tile .list__meta ic--forward

    The <a> is the row, as in the card's list rows: a tap anywhere lands, and it is one tab stop. Its name is everything in it, so the title goes first. The chevron says "goes somewhere"; a row that doesn't, doesn't get one.

    2.5

    Settings row

    A setting that takes effect at once, among others.

    .switch in a .list__rows item

    The row is Switch's own markup, whole: its label is the row and the target, and help goes under it. The list only adds its padding and the rules.

    2.6

    Row with actions

    Things you also rename, copy or delete: a list of decks.

    .list__actions .btn--icon .menu

    A More button after the row opens a Menu: Rename, Duplicate, Export, Delete deck…. Its name says whose actions they are ("More for Shapes"). If an app adds swipe (gate 4, or its own), the swipe offers these same actions and the button stays: without script, the button is all there is. The row keeps its link; the chevron goes, so the row doesn't end in two marks.

    03

    States

    Only a link row has states. No lift: a shadow would fall across the next row. Hover underlines the title; press fills the row with ink. A settings row's states are Switch's; the More button's are Button's.

    Usage

    1. Do

      Make the whole row the link when it goes somewhere, title first. Put every action a row has behind a visible More button, and name it after the row ("More for Shapes").

    2. Don't

      Don't make swipe the only way to an action, and don't put a chevron on a row that doesn't go anywhere. Don't repeat one glyph down every row: a lead says something or it goes.

    3. Installed PWA

      A plain list runs under the screen's gutter to both edges; the frame, not the list, keeps clear of the notch. Press shows on touch with the shell's touchstart listener. Swipe, if an app adds it, waits for gate 4.

    4. Mac and SwiftUI

      A List with our row as a custom view; on the Mac a selectable collection is a List or Table, so ⌘ and ⇧ selection come free, and the More menu is also a context menu and a menu bar item.

    01

    Anatomy

    A row of tabs on a rule, and under it the section they show. Not the segmented control: that switches how one thing is shown; tabs switch which section is shown.

    Usage

    Variants

    Three parts: the summary (the target), the glyph and the body. A disclosure is a ruled row; stacked, neighbours share a rule, so a group needs no wrapper.

    1.1

    Single

    One thing most people won't need: a how-it-works, a card's notes.

    The summary is the whole row, at least 44px: words first, the glyph at the end. ic--down swaps to ic--up when it's open, a static glyph, no turn. In a card it takes the card's ink, so it works on every tone.

    How spaced repetition works

    Cards you know come back less often: tomorrow, then in three days, then in a week. Cards you miss come back sooner, so your time goes where it's needed.

    Shapes · card 6 of 12

    Show the answer's notes

    Six sides and six corners. Bees build their combs from them.

    Group

    A list of questions, each answered in place: Help.

    .disclosure + .disclosure

    Disclosures one after another, each opening on its own. They share their rules, so the group reads as one ruled list. Put a heading over it; the summaries are not headings.

    What counts as known?

    A card is known once you get it right three sessions running.

    Can I study offline?

    Yes. Your decks are saved on this device, so a session works anywhere.

    Why did a card come back so soon?

    You marked it Not yet, so it comes back later in the same session.

    How do I start a deck again?

    Open the deck, then Settings, then Start again. The cards stay; only what you know is cleared.

    Menu

    A short list of actions behind one button. The browser's own popover opens it, closes it on Escape or a tap outside, and gives focus back. No script.

    01

    Anatomy

    A button, and a framed box of quiet buttons that opens under it. Shown here in place, as an open one looks.

    1
    2
    4
    1. 1
      Button.btn popovertarget

      Button, icon-only with ic--more and a name that says whose actions ("More for Shapes"), or with words ("Sort"). It stays down while its menu is open. The browser tells screen readers it's expanded.

    2. 2
      Surface.menu popover

      A container, so square: a 2px frame on paper, 8px inside, and no shadow, since a shadow means "press this". Under the button, end edges aligned; above it when there's no room.

    3. 3
      Item.menu__item

      Button, quiet and full width, words at the start. It closes the menu itself (popovertargetaction="hide"); the app's click does the rest. One to three words, a verb first.

    4. 4
      Rule.menu__rule

      An <hr>, 1px, the menu's whole width: it keeps the destructive item apart.

    5. 5
      Destructive item

      Last, after the rule. The words carry it, never a colour: "Delete deck…". The ellipsis promises a question before anything goes.

    02

    Variants

    One menu, two kinds of button. Both are live: open them with a click, Enter or Space; Tab moves through the items; Escape closes and puts you back on the button.

    2.1

    More

    A thing's other actions: a deck's Rename, Duplicate, Export, Delete.

    .btn--icon ic--more .menu .menu__item .menu__rule

    The button names the menu's id in popovertarget, and the menu comes right after it in the markup: Tab goes from the button into the menu and on. Four items or so; past seven, it's a screen.

    Sort

    A choice that changes how a list is ordered, behind a button with words.

    03

    States

    The button's and the items' states are Button's. The menu itself has two: closed and open, and where it opens. Shown in place here.

    Closed. Just the button, quiet. Hover and focus are Button's: a frame, a lift, the ring.

    Open. The button stays down; the menu hangs under it, end edges aligned, 4px off.

    Item, hover. Button's quiet hover: the pill fills and lifts. Pointers only.

    Item, focus. The hover look and the 3px ring, as on any button. Tab and Shift-Tab move it.

    Item, pressed. Down and filled, with the inner ring. Then the menu closes.

    Current choice. A check and Button's selected ring, never a fill: a fill is a press.

    Where it opens: under the button, end edges aligned; over it, or the other way along, when there's no room; at very large text sizes, centred over the button at the screen's height. Where CSS anchor positioning isn't supported it is a sheet across the bottom of the screen. The .is-* classes force a state for this page and for tests; they are not API.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

      Keep it short, verbs first, and put a destructive item last, after the rule, in words that say what goes: "Delete deck…", then ask or offer Undo.

    2. Don't

      Don't hide the only way to do something in a menu or a swipe; don't nest menus; don't give the menu a shadow or round corners. It isn't an ARIA menu, so don't add role="menu" without the arrow keys that promise.

    3. Installed PWA

      Anchored to its button on a phone too; a sheet at the bottom where anchoring isn't there. Light dismiss works with a tap anywhere outside, and Escape on a keyboard.

    4. Mac and SwiftUI

      Menus are system chrome: SwiftUI's Menu, a context menu, and every item in the menu bar with its shortcut. This element is the phone's and the web's.

    Taller than the room. At 90% of the screen it stops growing: the top bar stays and the body scrolls inside, never the page.

    Escape closes any sheet with no value. Under forced colours the scrim disappears and the frame on the edge facing the page goes to 4px. The last picture is held short with an inline height to stand for a small screen. The .is-* classes force a state for this page; they are not API.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

      Use a sheet for a short task that belongs to the screen under it, such as adding a card to this deck. Title it with the task, keep Close in view, and end the form with its own button.

    2. Don’t

      Don’t open a sheet from a sheet, or make a drag the only way out. A question is a Dialog, news is a Toast or a Banner, and a task with screens of its own is a screen with a back link, not a sheet.

    3. Installed PWA

      From the bottom, edge to edge, owning the home indicator’s safe area; at most 90% of the screen, so the deck still shows above it. On a phone, a thing’s actions open as an action sheet; on a wide window, as a Menu. Drag and detents wait for gate 4.

    4. Mac and SwiftUI

      Sheets are system chrome on the Mac: SwiftUI’s .sheet, with .inspector for a side panel and .confirmationDialog for an action sheet. This element is the phone’s and the web shell’s.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

      Say what happened in a few words, past tense, and offer the one thing worth doing about it. Raise it after the work is done, and after any dialog or sheet has closed: the page behind a modal is inert, and so is its region.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

    2. Don't

      Don't float it, pin it or lay it over content; don't give the offline banner a close; don't use one for "it's done" (that's a Toast) or for a question (that's a Dialog). No tinted fill to say what kind: the glyph and the words say it.

      Wave 5's service worker raises offline and update ready for real. Keep the band in the markup, empty, and fill it: a live region speaks when it changes, not when it arrives. Empty, it takes no room and draws nothing.

      The same band at the top of the window's content, under the toolbar, scrolling with it: in SwiftUI, the first row of the ScrollView, not a safeAreaInset, which would pin it.

    States

    One screen moves between the patterns. What shows, what a screen reader hears, and where focus is at each moment. Nothing moves on screen until gate 4: each appears in place.

    1. Opening, the first 300ms

      Shows: Nothing new: the bars are already there.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Where it was.

    2. Still loading

      Shows: The spinner and “Loading decks…” where the content will be.

      Heard: “Loading decks…”, politely, once.

      Focus: Where it was.

    3. Loaded

      Shows: The decks, in place of the spinner.

      Heard: Nothing: they're there when you look.

      Focus: Where it was.

    4. Loaded, nothing there

      Shows: “No decks yet.” and the ghost card.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Where it was; the ghost card is the next stop.

    5. Didn't load

      Shows: The plain card, Try again in its foot.

      Heard: At once (role="alert").

      Focus: Where it was; Try again is the next stop.

    6. Trying again

      Shows: The card stays; Try again goes busy, its label kept.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: On Try again. When the decks come, on the scroll region (the screen's <main>), so it isn't lost.

    7. Searching, no match

      Shows: The no-match line and Clear search, under the field.

      Heard: The line, politely, each time the list changes.

      Focus: In the field.

    8. Search cleared

      Shows: The field empties; the decks come back.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Back in the field.

    9. Offline

      Shows: The offline banner first, the decks on this device under it.

      Heard: “You're offline. Changes are saved on this device.”, politely, once.

      Focus: Where it was.

    10. Online again

      Shows: The banner goes.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Where it was.

    11. First run

      Shows: One line, one action, no bars to wander off with.

      Heard: The heading and the line, read in order.

      Focus: The action is the first stop.

    At 200% text each pattern wraps and grows taller, never wider. In forced colours the cards' and the banner's frames and rules, the ghost card's dashes and every glyph stay, in system colours.

    Usage

    1. Do

      Say what's going on, where the content would be, and offer the way forward. Keep the bars: a state is the content of a screen, never a screen without its way back.

    2. Don't

      Don't leave a screen blank, don't shimmer or draw skeleton boxes, don't say "Something went wrong" on its own, and don't say one failure twice (a banner and a card).

    3. Installed PWA

      Never blank (STYLE.md §4): empty is a ghost card offering the first step; an error is a plain card with Try again in its foot. Offline is not an error: show what's on the device, under the banner.

      The same patterns in the window's content. SwiftUI's ContentUnavailableView is the native one; we draw ours from the cards instead, because it centres a large symbol, which is decoration here. Loading is a ProgressView with its words.

    Element 27ColourGates 0 to 3 done

    PWA

    What turns the elements into an app on a home screen: it installs, works offline, updates when you say so, asks before it notifies, shares, and makes room for the keyboard. No new parts. Each pattern is made of elements you already have, and pwa.js switches it on where the browser can.

    01

    Anatomy

    A few files and a little script. The screens are made of elements; the manifest tells the home screen what the app is; the service worker keeps it on the device; and pwa.js, in dist/flashcards.min.js, connects the screen to both.

    1.1

    The platform, working

    A starter app to copy: three root screens, installable, and working offline.

    design/pwa/

    Copy it with dist/ and fonts/ to start an app. It installs and works offline only when it's served: run node design/tools/serve.mjs and open it on localhost, which counts as secure. Opened from disk it shows the screen, with no worker behind it.

    • index.htmlToday, the root screen: Frame and the Tab bar, one Banner waiting at the top for offline and updates, and an empty state that offers the first deck.
    • decks.html, settings.htmlDecks, with the New deck Sheet. Settings: the reminder card, Install and Share, export, import and the quota, and the iOS install Sheet.
    • manifest.webmanifestWhat the home screen knows: the name, the icons, the colour behind the splash, where the app starts and how far it reaches (1.2).
    • icons/A master SVG and a maskable one, and the PNGs rendered once from them (1.2).
    • sw.jsThe service worker: keeps the app on the device, and hands over to a new version only when you say (1.3).
    • offline.htmlWhat a page you've never opened shows when there's no connection.
    • app.jsThe starter's own code, the part an app replaces: decks kept on the device, export and import.
    Open the starter app

    1.2

    Manifest and icons

    What the browser and the home screen know about the app before it runs.

    manifest.webmanifest <link rel="manifest">

    The two colours are --canvas: tools/bundle.mjs writes them in from the colour file, so the hex lives in one place and the splash, the status bar and the first frame are one ground. A manifest has no dark colour, so it keeps the light canvas; the pages' two theme-color metas, light and dark, follow the system. Icons: one master SVG on the icon grid, ink on paper in both schemes (monochrome until an app sets its accent), its drawing inside the maskable safe zone, the centre 80% circle. The PNGs are rendered once from it, at 192 and 512 (any and maskable) and 180 for apple-touch-icon, which iOS reads instead of the manifest's icons.

    • idWhich app this is, so moving start_url later doesn't make a second one. A plain name: "./" would resolve to the bare origin."flashcards"
    • name, short_nameThe install sheet and the splash use the name; the home screen puts the short name under the icon, so 12 letters at most.Flashcards
    • descriptionOne line under the name in the install sheet: “Short daily sessions with your own decks of cards. Works offline.”
    • start_urlWhere it opens from the home screen: the root screen, never a deep page."./"
    • scopeHow far the app reaches. A link inside it stays in the app; a link outside opens in the browser."./"
    • lang, dirThe language and direction of the name and descriptions."en", "auto"
    • displayIts own window, with none of the browser's bars. So every screen past the root needs a back link (2.9)."standalone"
    • orientationNever locked: it turns with the phone, and a tablet works both ways (2.10)."any"
    • theme_color, background_colorThe status bar or title bar, and the splash while it opens. The light canvas: a manifest has no dark one.--canvas
    • iconsThe home screen, the app switcher and the splash. A maskable icon keeps its drawing in the safe zone, so a launcher's circle or squircle never cuts it.SVG, 192, 512
    • shortcutsA long press on the icon goes straight there.Today, Decks
    • screenshotsChromium's richer install sheet shows them.Narrow, wide

    1.3

    The service worker

    What sw.js keeps on the device, how it answers, and how it hands over to a new version.

    sw.js <meta name="flashcards-sw">

    pwa.js registers the worker the meta names, and only then: a page without the meta, like this one, never gets a worker. tools/bundle.mjs stamps the worker's version from the shell files' hash, so changing any of them makes a new worker, and changing none doesn't.

    • The shellThe starter's pages, flashcards.min.css, flashcards.min.js, the font and the icons. Cached when the worker installs, under its version, and served from there first: it opens at once, with or without a connection.
    • Anything else on the same originStale while revalidate: the cached copy now, a fresh one saved for next time. Fast, and never more than one visit out of date.
    • A page never cached, offlineoffline.html (2.3), never the browser's own error page.
    • Anything on another originNot touched: no respondWith, straight to the network. The worker never stands between the app and someone else's server.
    1. A new worker waits

      It installs beside the old one, which keeps running the open app.

    2. The band says so

      The update Banner shows: "A new version is ready." with Reload (2.2).

    3. Reload hands over

      It posts SKIP_WAITING to the waiting worker, which takes over.

    4. One reload

      On controllerchange the page reloads, once. Never on its own: you might be halfway through a card.

    1.4

    The hooks

    What pwa.js looks for in the markup, and what it does there.

    js/components/pwa.js data-pwa data-share

    Everything is detected by feature, never by browser name, and switched on by markup. Anything it drives ships hidden, so without script, or where the browser can't, nothing shows that wouldn't work.

    • <meta name="flashcards-sw" content="sw.js">Registers that worker. No meta, no worker.The page
    • data-pwa="offline"Fills the band while the browser is offline, and empties it after.A Banner
    • data-pwa="update"Fills the band, with a Reload Button (data-pwa="reload"), when a new worker waits. Reload hands over and reloads once. One band may take both: data-pwa="offline update".A Banner
    • data-pwa="install"Shows when installing is possible: replays Chromium's install prompt, or on iOS opens the Sheet its commandfor names. Never when standalone, never on load.A Button
    • data-shareOpens the share sheet with data-share-title and data-share-url, or copies the link and raises a Toast, “Link copied.”A Button
    • data-pwa="notify-ask"Shows while notifications haven't been asked for. Its data-pwa="notify" Button asks.A Card
    • data-pwa="notify-denied"Shows when the browser blocks notifications: how to allow them.Words
    • data-pwa="quota"Gets “Using 2.1 MB of 1.2 GB on this device.”A line
    • Flashcards.badge(n)Puts the count on the app's icon; 0 clears it.Script
    • Flashcards.persist()Asks the browser to keep the app's data when the device is short of room.Script
    • Flashcards.download(name, data)Saves data as a JSON file.Script
    • Flashcards.readJSON(file)Reads a chosen file back.Script
    02

    Patterns

    Eleven, made of Card, Button, List, Banner, Sheet, Switch, Field, Toast, Meter and Frame. Each live specimen is wired to pwa.js and shows only where this browser can do the thing; the markup printed is its own. Beside it, a still picture of every state, so the page reads the same without script.

    2.1

    Install

    Offer to install, in Settings, and only when the browser can.

    data-pwa="install" commandfor .sheet ic--install

    A row in Settings, hidden until it can work: the row and its Button both carry the hook. In Chromium the Button replays the browser's own install prompt, kept from beforeinstallprompt. iOS has no prompt, so on an iPhone the Button opens a Sheet with the steps. Installed, it never shows. Never a pop-up on load.

    This app

    • Works offline Your decks are kept on this device, so it opens without a connection.
    • Install Flashcards It opens from your home screen, full screen.

    Update

    A new version has downloaded: say so, and swap it in when the person chooses.

    data-pwa="update" data-pwa="reload" .banner ic--refresh

    Banner's update ready, at the top of the scroll region. Reload hands over to the new worker and the page reloads once. Left alone, the band waits: the new version also starts the next time the app opens from scratch. Nothing ever reloads by itself.

    Ask for notifications only after something the person did, and say what they'll get.

    2.7

    Keyboard

    Make room for the on-screen keyboard, and keep the field you're typing in above it.

    interactive-widget=resizes-content data-keyboard .frame

    Every page's viewport meta adds interactive-widget=resizes-content, so Android shrinks the page above the keyboard instead of covering it. A focused field scrolls clear with Frame's scroll padding. While the keyboard is up the Tab bar hides, where the browser shows it: frame.js sees the keyboard as lost viewport height (visualViewport) and sets data-keyboard on the frame. Elsewhere the bar stays.

    2.8

    Storage

    Keep the decks on the device, let them leave it as a file, and say how much room they take.

    Flashcards.persist() Flashcards.download() Flashcards.readJSON() data-pwa="quota"

    Ask the browser to keep the data through cleanup (Flashcards.persist()) after real use, never on first launch: the starter asks when the first deck is saved and after an import. Chromium decides without asking; Firefox asks. Export saves every deck as one JSON file; Import reads one back and says what it added, or why it couldn't. The quota line lives in Settings.

    Standalone

    An installed app has no browser around it: no back, no address, no refresh.

    .topbar__back ic--arrow display-mode: standalone

    Every screen past the root has Top bar's back. A link that leaves the app opens in the browser, and says so with ↗ (ic--arrow) and its words. A deep link inside scope opens that screen, with a back link to the root; the home screen always opens start_url. Install hides.

    2.11

    Performance budget

    What a served app downloads the first time, and the most it may.

    dist/flashcards.min.css dist/flashcards.min.js tools/bundle.mjs

    tools/bundle.mjs writes flashcards.min.css and flashcards.min.js (comments and spare whitespace out, nothing else), which a served app links, prints the gzipped sizes and fails the build over budget. First load on a mid-range phone stays under 2.5s to the largest paint, a target measured on a device; after that, the worker makes every load instant.

    CSS, gzipped About 13 of 30 KB
    Script, gzipped About 6 of 10 KB
    The font 88 of 90 KB

    Measured on 2026-10-20 with this wave's script in. The commented flashcards.js is 9.9 KB gzipped, so the budget is the min file's. The font is already compressed, so its file size is the number; preload it in a served app, with crossorigin. A KB is 1024 bytes. tools/bundle.mjs prints these on every build.

    03

    States

    What the app shows, what a screen reader hears, and where focus is, as the platform changes under it. Nothing moves on screen until gate 4: each appears in place.

    1. Offline

      Shows: The offline band first in the scroll region; everything on the device under it.

      Heard: "You're offline. Changes are saved on this device.", politely, once.

      Focus: Where it was.

    2. Online again

      Shows: The band goes.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Where it was.

    3. Update waiting

      Shows: The update band, with Reload.

      Heard: "A new version is ready.", politely, once.

      Focus: Where it was; Reload is the first stop in the content.

    4. Reloaded

      Shows: The same screen, on the new version, with the band gone.

      Heard: The page, from the top, as after any reload.

      Focus: At the top.

    5. Installable

      Shows: Install in Settings, beside the version. Nowhere else.

      Heard: Nothing until you reach it.

      Focus: Where it was.

    6. Installing

      Shows: Chromium's own install sheet; on iOS, the Sheet with the steps.

      Heard: The browser's sheet, or the Sheet's title.

      Focus: In the sheet; back on Install when it closes.

    7. Not asked yet

      Shows: After a session, the reminder card with Not now and Turn on.

      Heard: Nothing: it's there when you look.

      Focus: Where it was; the card's buttons come next.

    8. Asked

      Shows: The browser's prompt. Then the card goes; if the answer was no, the setting says how to allow it.

      Heard: The browser's prompt.

      Focus: Back on the page, at the scroll region, since the card has gone.

    9. Link copied

      Shows: Toast's done, "Link copied.", for 6 seconds.

      Heard: "Link copied.", politely.

      Focus: On Share.

    10. Keyboard up

      Shows: The Tab bar goes; the field you're in stays above the keyboard.

      Heard: Nothing new: the bar is out of the way, not announced.

      Focus: In the field.

    11. Keyboard down

      Shows: The Tab bar is back.

      Heard: Nothing.

      Focus: Where it was.

    12. Imported

      Shows: A Toast: "Added 2 decks from the file." The decks are there.

      Heard: The Toast, politely.

      Focus: On Import.

    At 200% text each pattern wraps and grows taller, never wider. In forced colours the bands' rules, the cards' and toasts' frames, the switch's knob and every glyph stay, in system colours.

    04

    Usage

    1. Do

      Ask for things after the person did something that needs them: notifications after a session, keeping the data after real use. Keep every count and setting inside the app too, and keep Install in Settings.

    2. Don't

      Don't prompt on load, reload without asking, lock the orientation, or show Install to an installed app. Don't badge what the app doesn't also show, or let the worker touch another origin's requests.

    3. Installed PWA

      Install, web push and the keyboard behave differently on iOS, and only a device shows how: an iPhone installs through Add to Home Screen, gets push only once installed, and lays the keyboard over the page. Each is marked as needing a device in the spec.

    4. Mac and SwiftUI

      Installed from Chrome or Safari (File, Add to Dock), the app gets its own window and Dock icon, and the badge goes on the Dock icon. Natively these are the system's: the App Store installs, UNUserNotificationCenter asks, ShareLink shares.
